title: Vaisakhi, the harvest
hookLine: the spring harvest festival, and the founding of the Khalsa in 1699

lines: A HARVEST, AND A SECOND STORY.
cards: Mid-April in Punjab. The wheat has turned gold and it's time to cut it. Farmers have waited all winter, and when the harvest comes in there's drumming, dancing, the big swinging steps of bhangra.
Communities across north India keep this harvest festival. But for Sikhs, the same day carries a second story, one that changed the shape of their whole community on a single morning in 1699.
On the last day of this visit to Sikhism: Vaisakhi.

teach.b: Vaisakhi takes its name from Vaisakh, a month in the Indian calendar, and it falls in mid-April. Here's the story Sikhs tell.
In 1699 the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, called Sikhs to gather at Anandpur. Before the crowd he drew a sword and asked: who will give his head for the faith? Silence.
Then one man stood up. The Guru led him into a tent and came out alone, the sword wet. He asked again.
Another stood. Five times. Tellings differ about what happened inside the tent, but they agree on the ending: the five came out alive, dressed in new clothes.
Sikhs call them the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones. They came from different castes and different regions, and that mattered deeply.
The Guru stirred water and sugar in an iron bowl with a double-edged sword, and tradition says his wife added the sweetness.

With this amrit he initiated the five into the Khalsa, a community of committed Sikhs, and gave the men the name Singh, lion. Women who take amrit are named Kaur, often rendered princess. Then the surprise.

teach.h: THE GURU ASKS THE FIVE TO INITIATE HIM.
teach.b: The Guru knelt and asked the five to initiate him.

The teacher became a student of his own students. Put the two stories together, the harvest and the Khalsa, and you get a festival about beginnings: a field that starts over, and a community that started over.
A good end to a week that began with one creator, then the name, honest work, sharing, the kitchen and rising spirits.

how: Sikhs mark Vaisakhi with worship at the gurdwara, processions called nagar kirtan, langar, and often amrit initiation ceremonies; in Punjab it is also a harvest celebration.

games.q: you are Guru Gobind Singh. five have given everything and been initiated. what now?
o: kneel and ask them to initiate you.
games.why: Sikhs tell that the Guru asked the five to give him amrit too: the leader joined the community on the same terms.

practice: Think of one thing in your life that is starting over, or could: a job, a friendship after a gap, a habit, a morning. Hold it the way a farmer looks at a field after the harvest: cleared, open, ready.
Breathe in and let it be new; breathe out and let last season go.

wordCard.voice: Vaisakhi. The April harvest festival, and for Sikhs the day the Khalsa was founded in 1699. Today's word.
